content: Hepatitis C is a significant contributor to liver-related illness and death. Many individuals with the condition remain asymptomatic throughout their lives. The standard treatment for chronic hepatitis C involves a combination of peginterferon and ribavirin. However, in certain cases, ribavirin monotherapy has been considered as an alternative treatment option. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of ribavirin monotherapy in patients with chronic hepatitis C. To achieve this, clinical trials were identified through electronic databases, manual searches of bibliographies and journals, direct communication with trial authors, and inquiries to pharmaceutical companies. The search included studies up to March 2009. The study included all randomized trials, regardless of blinding, language, or publication status, that compared ribavirin monotherapy to no intervention, placebo, or interferon therapy in patients with chronic hepatitis C. The primary outcomes assessed were sustained virological response (defined as the absence of detectable hepatitis C virus RNA at least six months after treatment), liver-related morbidity and all-cause mortality, and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included virological response at the end of treatment, biochemical response (measured by transaminase activity), and histological response. The study also evaluated randomization methods, blinding, data handling, and funding sources to assess the risk of bias. Both random-effects and fixed-effect meta-analyses were conducted, with results from the fixed-effect model presented when both models yielded the same statistical significance. A total of 14 randomized trials involving 657 patients were included in the analysis. Most of these trials had unclear methods for controlling bias. When compared to placebo or no intervention, ribavirin monotherapy did not significantly improve sustained virological response (risk difference [RD] 0%, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2% to 3%, based on five trials) or virological response at the end of treatment (RD 0%, 95% CI -3% to 3%, based on ten trials). Additionally, ribavirin monotherapy had no significant impact on liver-related morbidity or mortality (RD 0%, 95% CI -2% to 3%, based on 11 trials). However, ribavirin monotherapy was associated with a significant increase in adverse reactions, particularly anemia. While ribavirin did improve biochemical and histological responses at the end of treatment, it did not result in sustained biochemical improvement. Furthermore, ribavirin monotherapy was found to be significantly less effective than interferon monotherapy in achieving virological and biochemical responses (based on five trials). In conclusion, ribavirin monotherapy does not appear to provide meaningful benefits in terms of sustained virological response, liver-related morbidity, or mortality. It is associated with a higher risk of adverse effects and is significantly less effective than interferon monotherapy. Given the small number of patients included in the trials and the limitations of the available data, further research may be necessary. However, based on the current evidence, ribavirin monotherapy cannot be recommended for the treatment of chronic hepatitis C outside the context of randomized clinical trials.
